title: Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, return all possible letter combinations that the digits could represent on a classic phone keypad. Explain the backtracking technique that fixes one digit's letter at a time.
shortTitle: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number (All Keypad Letter Combinations)

s1_definition.profdef: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number is a Subsets-pattern problem that enumerates the Cartesian product of the letter groups mapped to each digit. Using backtracking, we fix one letter for the first digit, recurse to fix a letter for the next digit, and so on until all digits are assigned, then record the combination. The number of results is the product of the group sizes, and the work is proportional to that output size.

Each digit offers a small group of letters, like 2 maps to a, b, c. We pick one letter for the first digit, then one for the next, building up every full spelling by trying all choices at each position.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Letter Combinations of a Phone Number is a Subsets-pattern problem that enumerates the Cartesian product of the letter groups mapped to each digit. Using backtracking, we fix one letter for the first digit, recurse to fix a letter for the next digit, and so on until all digits are assigned, then record the combination. The number of results is the product of the group sizes, and the work is proportional to that output size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, customers sometimes remember a vanity branch phone code by its letters, and support wants every letter spelling a digit code could map to, so they can match it against known branch words. Each digit offers a small group of letters, like 2 maps to a, b, c. We pick one letter for the first digit, then one for the next, building up every full spelling by trying all choices at each position.

**One line to remember:** For each digit try every mapped letter, recurse to the next digit, and record a combination when all digits are assigned.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a mapping from each digit character to its letter group, for example digit 2 maps to the string "abc". We recurse with an index into the digit string and a builder for the current combination. At each level we look up the letters for the current digit and loop over them; for each letter we append it, recurse to the next index, then remove it to try the next letter.

When the index reaches the end of the digit string we have assigned a letter to every digit, so we record the combination, for example `result.add(current.toString());`. An empty input returns an empty result rather than a single empty string, which is the conventional edge case.

A senior-level nuance is that this is exactly a Cartesian product, and the backtracking depth equals the number of digits, so the recursion is shallow even though the output can be large. Another nuance is that digits 7 and 9 map to four letters while others map to three, so the per-digit branching is not uniform, and the total count is the product of these group sizes.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs vanity branch phone codes, and support wants every letter spelling of a short digit code to match against a dictionary of branch words. This is exactly how Letter Combinations works: each digit contributes a group of letters and we enumerate all spellings.

Problem 2 — Spelling out combinations by hand is error-prone and misses options. This is why we backtrack over the digit positions, trying every letter at each position, which guarantees all spellings appear.

The code defines a `PhoneLetterService` exposing `letterCombinations(digits)` returning all spellings. A `Demo` runs it over a two-digit code and logs the combinations.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: digit code 23.

Step 1: The first digit 2 maps to a, b, c. Choose a and recurse to the second digit.

Step 2: The second digit 3 maps to d, e, f. For the current prefix a, append d, e, f in turn, recording "ad", "ae", "af". Backtrack to the first digit.

Step 3: Choose b for the first digit, then d, e, f for the second, recording "bd", "be", "bf".

Step 4: Choose c for the first digit, then d, e, f, recording "cd", "ce", "cf".

Step 5: The nine spellings are ad, ae, af, bd, be, bf, cd, ce, cf, which is three times three.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Letter Combinations of a Phone Number enumerates every letter spelling that a string of keypad digits could represent, which is exactly the Cartesian product of the letter groups mapped to each digit. I solve it with backtracking: I keep a mapping from each digit to its letters, and I recurse over the digit positions. At each position I loop over the letters for that digit, appending one, recursing to the next position, and then removing it to try the next letter. When I have assigned a letter to every digit I record the completed spelling.

The point I make is that although the output can be large, the recursion depth is only the number of digits, so the search is shallow and the cost is proportional to the number of spellings it must produce. I also handle the conventional edge case where an empty input returns an empty list rather than a single empty string, and I note that digits seven and nine have four letters while the others have three, so the branching is non-uniform and the total count is the product of the group sizes.

At the National Bank of India I used this in support tooling for vanity branch phone codes, generating every letter spelling of a short digit code to match against a dictionary of branch words. I backtracked over the digit positions with an immutable keypad map and trimmed the builder after each branch. Explaining that this is a Cartesian product with shallow recursion and handling the empty-input case is what shows an interviewer that I recognise the Subsets pattern behind a classic keypad question.
